en: The Jātaka:
The Twelfth Chapter,
The Section on the Lesser Kuṇāla.
1. The Cūḷakuṇāla Jātaka “Of those who are greedy, fickle-minded,
ungrateful, and treacherous;”
A man who is not devoted to the gods is not worthy of trust;
they do not understand what has been done or what remains to be done.
Neither mother, nor father, nor brother—
those ignoble ones who have transcended the Dhamma—
fall under the sway of their own minds alone.
Even one who has lived with them for a long time, who is dear and pleasing,
compassionate, and as dear as life itself— their husband—
they abandon him during times of domestic necessity.
Therefore, I do not trust women.
For the mind of women is like that of a monkey,
like a tree's shadow that shifts from ear to ear.
The heart of women is fickle and unsteady;
it revolves like the rim of a wheel.
When they look upon [a man] with longing, [it turns toward him].
A man’s wealth consists of a form that is desirable;
they lead him away with gentle words,
as the people of Kamboja lead a horse by means of a lotus.
When those who look closely do not see any wealth of a man that is worth seizing,
they avoid him from every side.
Like one who has crossed over and reached the further shore,
he abandons the raft. Like fire to resin, like a fire-eating bird,
and like a river with a swift current, so are sharp deceit and guile.
These serve both the pleasant and the unpleasant,
just as a boat serves both this shore and the far shore;
they belong neither to one person nor to two.
Like a shop laid out for sale:
he who would think "these are mine" tries to catch the wind with a net.
Just as a river, a road,
a tavern, an assembly hall,
and a well— so too are women in the world.
No limit exists for them.
They are like jars placed on a stool,
resembling the heads of black snakes.
Just as cattle graze upon abundant grass,
each seeking the best for itself,
so do they approach the elephant with its trunk upraised, the black serpent, and—
An anointed king and all women—
a man should associate with these constantly,
for their true nature is indeed difficult to understand.
A woman of exquisite beauty is not dear to many;
a pampered wife should not be served for the sake of wealth,
nor should another's wife be pursued for the sake of riches.
“These five kinds of women should not be cultivated.
Thus ends the first story, the Cūḷakuṇālajātaka.
